properties.name: Fernald's Neck Preserve Lincolnville ME
properties.description: A 325-acre peninsula preserve in the middle of Megunticook Lake, mostly mature hardwoods, hemlocks, and pines. Three trails of varying length and difficulty, with shoreline swimming access via Balance Rock on the Orange/White trails. No dogs or hunting permitted. Originally donated to The Nature Conservancy in 1969, transferred to Coastal Mountains Land Trust in 2007.
properties.detail:
Fernald's Neck Preserve

📍 Fernalds Neck Road, Lincolnville ME (on Megunticook Lake)

A 325-acre peninsula preserve in the middle of Megunticook Lake, mostly mature hardwoods, hemlocks, and pines. Three trails of varying length and difficulty, with shoreline swimming access via Balance Rock on the Orange/White trails. No dogs or hunting permitted. Originally donated to The Nature Conservancy in 1969, transferred to Coastal Mountains Land Trust in 2007.

Tips
- White Trail (0.4mi, easy), Orange Trail (1.75mi, moderate, includes Balance Rock swimming access), Blue Trail (1.8mi, moderately difficult) — pick based on how much time/effort you want.
- Parking lot holds only 11-12 cars, gate open 6:30am-7:30pm — arrive early in peak season.
- This is the destination note's own namesake attraction — previously had no Place note at all.
- Coordinates above are an approximation — worth confirming the exact parking-lot location against Google Maps before you go.

Fernald’s Neck Preserve is a beautiful, quiet, lake-centered woodland hike near Camden—but it is not as effortless as Beech Hill or Merryspring. Go for mature pines, swimming spots, Balance Rock, and a genuinely wild-feeling peninsula on Megunticook Lake; expect roots, rocks, a few short steep sections, and no dogs.[1][2][3]

At a glance

- Location: Lincolnville, about 15 minutes north of Camden via Route 52/Mountain Street. From Camden, drive about 5.8 miles north on Route 52, turn left onto Fernalds Neck Road, stay left at the fork, and continue to the parking lot.[2][1]
- Size: 285 acres covering most of a peninsula extending into Megunticook Lake.[1][2]
- Trail network: About 3.8–4 miles total, with roughly 3 miles of protected shoreline.[3][4][2]
- Best features: Mature pine/hemlock forest, lake shore, swimming access, Great Bog wildlife habitat, rocky bluffs, and Balance Rock.[2][1]
- Dogs: Not allowed, except service animals; a few third-party listings are outdated or incorrect.[5][6][1]

The experience

The preserve feels notably more remote and forested than its distance from Camden suggests. The woods are dominated by big pines, hemlocks, and hardwoods, creating a cool, shaded understory with mossy rocks, fungi, and intermittent lake views.[1][2]

This is not a continuous shoreline promenade. You travel through the woods, then reach selected lake-access points, bluffs, and small rocky swimming spots—so it rewards people who take the network rather than simply walking to one viewpoint and leaving.[3][2]

What not to miss

Balance Rock

Balance Rock is a huge glacial erratic perched apparently precariously on bedrock. It is close to the trailhead—about 0.2 mile with only 19 feet of elevation gain—so it is an easy, worthwhile stop even if you do not do the full hike.[7][1]

Blue Trail bluff view

The Blue Trail has the preserve’s strongest scenic viewpoint: a high bluff with a broad lake view and a backdrop toward Mount Megunticook. The far end of this trail is one of the rockier and hillier parts of the network, but the view is the preserve’s best “high reward” payoff.[2][3]

Orange Trail lake access

The Orange Trail leads to shoreline access and a small beachy/rocky swimming area. It also includes Balance Rock, but it is among the more uneven and hilly routes, so wear proper walking shoes rather than sandals.[8][1][2]

Great Bog

Where the Blue and Orange trails run near Great Bog is the best zone for birding and wildlife watching. Watch the lake and shoreline for bald eagles and other water-dependent wildlife.[2]

White Trail lake access

The short White Trail is the easiest route: 0.4 mile round trip. Use it for a quick, low-effort route to the lake, especially if you want to swim or simply sit at the water rather than undertake the more rugged loop.[1]

Trail choices

| Route | Distance | Difficulty | Best for |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Balance Rock spur | ~0.2 mi | Easy | Quick landmark stop, minimal effort [7] |
| White Trail | 0.4 mi round trip | Easy | Fastest route to lake access [1] |
| Blue Trail | 1.8 mi round trip | Moderate | Best bluff view and a satisfying shorter hike [1][3] |
| Orange Trail | 1.75 mi round trip | Moderate | Swimming access, rocky shoreline, Balance Rock [1][2] |
| Main loop / Blue + Orange combination | ~3.5–4 mi | Easy-moderate | The full experience: forest, bog, lake, bluff, and swimming spots [2][8] |

How hard is it?

The preserve is officially a mix of easy and moderate routes, and that is accurate. Its main challenge is footing, not sustained elevation: exposed roots, rocks, and a couple of short climbs to bluffs.[9][3][1]

A common 1.9-mile loop is rated easy with about 98 feet of gain, but the Blue and Orange Trail outer sections become rougher and hillier. If you are comfortable with natural forest paths and can manage uneven ground, it is very manageable; if you want paved, flat, or obstacle-free walking, choose Round Top Farm, Salt Bay Farm, or Merryspring instead.[10][11][12][2]

Best route for you

The complete but sensible outing

Allow 1.5 to 2 hours and take the Blue Trail toward the scenic bluff, then use the Orange Trail to reach the lake and swimming area, stopping at Balance Rock near the beginning or end. This gives you every major payoff without trying to turn the outing into a long-distance hike.[3][2]

The lighter version

Walk to Balance Rock, take the short White Trail to the lake, then return. It is the best choice if you want quiet forest and water scenery with the least physical effort.[7][1]

Practical details

- Parking: Limited—roughly 11–12 vehicles—at the end of a narrow, winding dirt road. Park only in the designated lot, not along the road.[3][1]
- Gate: Listed as opening at 6:30 AM and closing promptly at 7:30 PM. Do not risk returning late to a locked gate.[1][2]
- Footwear: Trail shoes or hiking shoes are advisable; skip flip-flops, especially on the Blue and Orange trails.[8][3]
- Swimming: Bring water shoes or sturdy sandals if you plan to enter the lake—the shore access is rocky rather than a groomed beach.[3][1]
- Cell coverage / facilities: Treat it as a simple backcountry-style preserve: no facilities or staffed visitor center are listed, so bring water, insect repellent, and a downloaded map.[2][1]
- Check before driving: Coastal Mountains Land Trust notes that unpaved-road access and trail conditions can lead to temporary closures, particularly during mud season.[4]

Bottom line

Fernald’s Neck is best when you want a more immersive, uncrowded, wooded-and-water experience than a pure scenic overlook. It is one of the better hidden-gem walks near Camden, but choose it for natural forest, lake swimming, and a moderate amount of uneven footing—not for a completely easy stroll.[2][3]

properties.name: First Connecticut Lake Pittsburg NH
properties.description: At 3,071 acres, the largest and lowest-elevation of the four Connecticut Lakes, at the true headwaters of the Connecticut River. Landlocked salmon and lake trout fishing, with fly-fishing-only stretches where the river enters; three public boat launches, ice fishing January–March.
properties.detail:
First Connecticut Lake

📍 Pittsburg, NH

The largest and lowest of the four Connecticut Lakes at 3,071 acres — the eighth-largest lake entirely within New Hampshire, sitting right at the headwaters of the Connecticut River. Known for landlocked salmon and lake trout; the fly-fishing-only stretch where the river enters the lake (Magalloway Bridge to Green's Point) is a spring and fall favorite. Three public boat launches provide access; ice fishing runs January through March, with average ice-out the first week of May.

Tips
- Bring fly gear if targeting the salmon run near the inlet — check current fly-fishing-only regulations before dropping bait or lures there.

properties.name: First Parish Church Congress St Portland ME
properties.description: Portland's finest example of Federal Period architecture, commissioned in 1824, featuring the last remaining functioning Simon Willard clock tower of its kind; the oldest place of worship in the city.
properties.detail:
First Parish Church (Congress St)

📍 425 Congress Street, Portland, ME

First Parish Church at 425 Congress Street is considered one of Portland's finest examples of Federal Period architecture. Commissioned in 1824 to replace a wooden meeting house called Old Jerusalem, its granite structure allowed it to survive the Great Fire of 1866.

One of the building's most notable features is the Simon Willard clock tower — the last remaining functioning clock tower of its kind.

Fun fact: First Parish Church is the oldest place of worship in the city of Portland.

Note: Also featured on the Hidden Public Spaces walking tour — see First Parish Church Portland ME for garden and tour details.

properties.name: First Parish Church Portland ME
properties.description: A stunning granite church built in 1825 at 425 Congress Street, housing a 600-pound cut-glass chandelier with a cannonball fused in its chain; public welcome in the surrounding gardens anytime.
properties.detail:
First Parish Church

First Parish Church at 425 Congress Street was built in 1825 to replace Old Jerusalem, the wooden predecessor on the same site. Inside this stunning granite building hangs a 600-pound cut-glass chandelier with a cannonball fused in the chain.

The church has partnered with Portland By The Foot to provide guided tours to the public. Even without a tour, the public is always welcome to enjoy the lovely gardens surrounding the church — a wonderful spot to pause and meditate.

Fun fact: The Maine Constitution was drafted in the original wooden church (Old Jerusalem) in 1820.

Highlights
- 600-pound cut-glass chandelier with embedded cannonball
- Peaceful surrounding gardens (always accessible)
- Guided tours available via Portland By The Foot
- Historic connection to the drafting of the Maine Constitution (1820)

properties.name: First Reformed Church Burial Ground Fishkill NY

Congregation formed 1716, began building in 1725 with help from Catharyna Brett, whose body rests under the pulpit. During the Revolution the NY Provincial Congress met here; the church became a Tory prison.
properties.detail:
First Reformed Church, Burial Ground

📍 Main St, Village of Fishkill, NY 12524

National Register listed. The church is the earliest house of worship in the county. The congregation, formed 1716, began building in 1725 with help from Catharyna Brett, whose body rests under the pulpit. During the Revolution the NY Provincial Congress met here as it formed a new government. The church became a Tory prison, where Enoch Crosby, the American secret agent who inspired Cooper's "The Spy," was imprisoned. At war's end ca. 1785, the devastated building was rebuilt and expanded — the steeple, dating from this era, is a village landmark.

Tips
- Stop 27 of 38 on the Beacon & Fishkill Heritage Tour (Tour 7).

properties.detail:
Fishkill Historic District

📍 Main St (NY-52), Fishkill, NY 12524

The historic core of Fishkill Village, roughly Main Street between Cary and Hopewell Streets — 108 buildings, mostly Greek Revival, dating from the late 18th to late 19th century. Listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1973. Once a key Revolutionary War crossroads tied to the nearby Fishkill Supply Depot, today it's a walkable strip of local shops and restaurants with its colonial-era character intact.

Tips
- Pairs naturally with Van Wyck Homestead, just down Route 9 — do them together as one stop.
- Best experienced as a short walk down Main Street rather than a single ticketed site.

properties.name: Flume Bridge Franconia Notch NH
properties.description: The Flume Gorge itself — an 800-foot natural chasm discovered in 1808, with boardwalks winding through granite walls to Avalanche Falls. One of Franconia Notch State Park's signature attractions, established as a park in 1928.
properties.detail:
Flume Gorge

📍 Flume Visitor Center, Franconia Notch State Park, NH

Discovered in 1808 by 93-year-old "Aunt" Jess Guernsey while fishing, this 800-foot granite gorge originally held a massive suspended boulder wedged between its walls — swept away by a violent 1883 rainstorm that also deepened the gorge and carved Avalanche Falls. Wooden boardwalks now wind through the chasm, crossing the Sentinel Pine Covered Bridge along the loop. A cornerstone of Franconia Notch State Park since its 1928 establishment.

Tips
- Ticketed attraction with its own visitor center — budget 1.5-2 hours for the full 2-mile loop.
- Can get crowded midday in summer/fall — early morning is best.

properties.detail:
Flume Cascade

📍 Route 302, Crawford Notch, NH

A roadside cascade along Route 302 in Crawford Notch, one of several waterfalls (with Silver Cascade nearby) visible right from pull-offs on the drive through the notch.

Tips

- A quick photo stop rather than a hike.

properties.name: Fore River Sanctuary Portland ME
properties.description: A 85-acre forested sanctuary managed by Portland Trails, featuring ~3 miles of easy wooded paths and Jewell Falls — Maine's only urban waterfall — tucked into a quiet ravine just minutes from downtown Portland.
properties.detail:
Fore River Sanctuary

📍 Rowe Avenue trailhead, Portland, ME

The Fore River Sanctuary is an 85-acre nature preserve managed by Portland Trails, just a few miles west of downtown. Its network of easy wooded paths winds through mature forest along the Fore River estuary — and at the heart of it sits Jewell Falls, Maine's only urban waterfall.

The falls are modest but genuinely lovely: a 26-foot cascade tucked into a shaded ravine, with a small footbridge and benches. The hike to the falls from the Rowe Avenue trailhead is under a mile each way and suitable for any fitness level.

Tips
- The full trail network is about 3 miles; the out-and-back to Jewell Falls is ~1.5 miles and takes 30–40 minutes
- Trailhead parking is on Rowe Avenue off Brighton Avenue — small lot, arrive early on weekends
- Bring bug spray in summer — the wetland sections can be buggy
- Dogs welcome on leash

Established October 1899 as a fixed red light to guide vessels through hazardous tidal currents at the Kennebec River's entrance, and upgraded in 1903 with a white pyramidal bell tower and 1,000-pound fog bell. Automation ended the staffed era in 1941, and the light was relocated onto adjacent Fort Popham in 1949 — a modern light still shines from a spindle atop the fort today.

Why go: Portland's most-photographed lighthouse plus walkable fort ruins on dramatic ocean cliffs — history and scenery in one stop.

Who it's for: Everyone — families, dog owners, photographers, history buffs. Genuinely broad appeal.

Frenchman Bay Lobster Rolls is a small takeout seafood establishment located on Main Street in Bar Harbor, Maine. The restaurant is known for its buttery lobster rolls served with generous portions and quality ingredients.

Visitors and cruise passengers passing through Bar Harbor seeking authentic Maine lobster rolls. Both locals and tourists frequent the spot, particularly those looking for casual, quick seafood dining with waterfront access.

properties.name: Fresh and Co Camden ME
properties.description: Upscale-casual, globally-inspired dinner spot in Camden — chef-owned, energetic room, known for lobster ravioli and Brazilian moqueca.
properties.detail:
Time: 2026-08-05T18:30:00

Fresh & Co in Camden is a strong pick if you want an upscale-casual dinner with globally inspired food, a lively room, and a menu that goes well beyond standard Maine seafood. The most consistently praised orders are the lobster ravioli, moqueca, mussels, and the house specialties that change with the season.[1][2][3][4]

What to order

The safest “best bets” are:

- Lobster ravioli — repeatedly called a signature dish and a longtime favorite.[3][5]
- Moqueca — a Brazilian coconut-lime seafood stew that reviewers have singled out as outstanding and very fresh.[2][4][6]
- Mussels — one of the restaurant’s most praised dishes, especially because they’re local and well-seasoned.[4][2][3]
- Rigatoni ala vodka — a good non-seafood choice if you want something richer and a little spicy.[6][2]
- Steak frites au poivre — best if you want a more classic, heartier main.[2]

For starters, the house dip with pita, crab & artichoke dip, or mussels are the strongest-sounding options from the current menu. If you want a lighter first course, the green salad or Caesar are fine, but they’re not the standout dishes here.[2]

What to expect

Expect a restaurant that feels more global and chef-driven than typical coastal Maine dining. Fresh & Co describes itself as globally inspired and locally sourced, with the menu shaped by travel, family roots, and local ingredients.[7][8][4]

The setting is part of the appeal: it’s energetic, often busy, and has a polished but not stiff atmosphere; several reviews mention strong service and a fun kitchen/dining-room buzz. Reservations are available, it opens at 5 pm, takeout is offered, and there is some outdoor seating when weather allows.[8][1][3][4]

Best fit for you

If you like adventurous food and don’t mind a menu that mixes Maine seafood with Brazilian, Eastern European, and Mediterranean influences, this is a very good choice. If you want a simple lobster-roll kind of place, it is probably not the best match because the menu is more eclectic and dinner-focused.[4][7][8][2]

For a first visit, I’d order the mussels or house dip to start, then the moqueca or lobster ravioli, and leave room for dessert if the menu leans seasonal that night.[9][3][2]

📍 Goat Island, Cape Porpoise, Kennebunkport, ME

Congress appropriated funds in 1831; the original tower was first lit in August 1833 and replaced by the current brick tower in 1859. It held onto its keeper the longest of any Maine light station, staffed until 1990. Transferred to the Kennebunkport Conservation Trust in 1998 under the Maine Lights Program.

Tips
- A small dock is usable for 1–2 hours around high tide; resident volunteer keepers offer summer tower tours.
- New England Eco Adventures runs guided boat tours with island landings.
- Best views otherwise are from the water.

properties.name: Good Wolf Northeast Harbor ME
properties.detail: Good Wolf is a women-owned restaurant in Northeast Harbor, Maine, known for its flavorful pizza and locally sourced dishes. The establishment attracts a mixed demographic, including friends dining together and those seeking a unique culinary experience. It has a casual yet stylish atmosphere and is regarded as a great addition to the local dining scene, offering a blend of upscale flavors in a friendly environment. Patrons consistently praise the amazing flavor of the pizza, the exceptional service, and the beautiful setting. Some reviews highlight that the restaurant's hours are limited, with several days being closed, which may be seen as a downside by potential diners.

properties.name: Goose Rocks Lighthouse Vinalhaven ME
properties.description: An 1890 "spark-plug" style iron lighthouse in the Fox Islands Thoroughfare between Vinalhaven and North Haven. Privately owned by Beacon Preservation, Inc., which offers paid overnight lodging.
properties.detail:
Goose Rocks Lighthouse

📍 Fox Islands Thoroughfare, between Vinalhaven and North Haven, ME

Completed November 14, 1890, this distinctive 37-foot "spark-plug" iron tower stands on a submerged ledge guarding a key shipping passage. Automated in 1963. In December 1940, substitute keeper Roy Manchester disappeared when his boat apparently exploded en route to the station.

Tips
- Privately owned by Beacon Preservation, Inc. — requires permission, though paid overnight stays are available.
- Isle au Haut Boat Services runs tours that pass the lighthouse; otherwise only reachable by water.

properties.name: Gorge Path Acadia National Park ME
properties.description: A narrow, forested gorge trail climbing the saddle between Cadillac and Dorr Mountains, following a seasonal stream past over 1,000 stone steps — one of Acadia's classic historic trails, with old-growth forest and ocean views from either summit.
properties.detail:
Gorge Path

📍 Off Park Loop Road, near the stone bridge over Kebo Brook, Acadia National Park ME

Climbs the narrow, shaded gorge between Cadillac Mountain and Dorr Mountain, staying close to a seasonal stream before the trail's signature feature: more than 1,000 stone steps built into the mountainside. Reaches the saddle between the two peaks, with ocean and island views available from either summit as an add-on.

Tips
- Coordinates are approximate — trailhead is on Park Loop Road's one-way section, right after crossing the stone bridge over Kebo Brook; roadside parking only
- Can be combined with a Cadillac Mountain or Dorr Mountain summit for full views
- Old-growth forest and the bubbling stream make it a good pick on a hot day, more shaded than most Acadia trails

Graffam Bros Seafood Market

A genuine local favorite seafood market founded in 1946, offering fresh catch sourced and frequented by locals rather than operating as a tourist fish shack. A true working market with authentic local clientele.

- Fresh catch from local sources
- Authentic local feel
- Good for picking up fresh seafood

Granite State Scenic Railway (Hobo Railroad)

properties.detail:
Granite Store

📍 Sullivan, ME

A historic store building in Sullivan, listed on the National Register of Historic Places — a reminder of the granite-quarrying industry that once drove this stretch of the Down East coast, shipping stone from Sullivan and Sullivan Harbor to build cities up and down the Eastern Seaboard.

- A quick roadside historical stop rather than an active retail store today.

properties.name: Grant Park Bar Harbor ME
properties.description: Named for Harry Allen Grant, who built the second-ever summer cottage in Bar Harbor here in 1869 as a wedding gift. The cottage was demolished in 1930; the Town purchased the land in 1912, and the Village Improvement Association developed it into today's public park in 1929.
properties.detail:
📍 Bar Harbor, ME, on the Shore Path — stop 7

Story

This little park is named for Harry Allen Grant, a New York lawyer who built the second-ever summer cottage in Bar Harbor, back in eighteen sixty-nine — the same opening years as Shore Acres, back near Derby Lane earlier on this walk. It was a wedding gift, and it cost him all of four hundred dollars for the land. The cottage itself is long gone, torn down in nineteen thirty — like Shore Acres, lost to the slow economics of the cottage era rather than to any single dramatic event.

The town bought this land in nineteen twelve, and it was the Village Improvement Association — the same organization that built the path you're standing on — that turned it into the public park you're looking at now, in nineteen twenty-nine.

The Village Improvement Association was founded by Charles T. How — see Bar Harbor City Narrative Bible for his full story (he also built The Turrets).

Audio

Once the script above is rendered in Fish Audio, embed the resulting file here, e.g. `!Grant Park narration.mp3` — Obsidian renders a native play button automatically, no plugin needed.

Granville Gulf State Reservation

properties.name: Great Duck Island Lighthouse Southwest Harbor ME
properties.description: An 1890 lighthouse ~8.5 miles southeast of Bass Harbor, now a biology and ecology field station run by College of the Atlantic. Closed to visitors spring through mid-fall.
properties.detail:
Great Duck Island Lighthouse

📍 Great Duck Island, ~8.5 miles southeast of Bass Harbor, ME

Placed in operation December 31, 1890 — a 42-foot cylindrical brick tower with a fifth-order lens flashing red. The fog signal here was one of the busiest in the state, sounding up to 1,542 hours a year. Assistant keeper Nathan Adam Reed raised sixteen children on the island and ran a one-room school in a converted barn.

Tips

- Lighthouse cruises from Bar Harbor or aerial flights from Bar Harbor airport offer views.

properties.name: Green Mount Cemetery Montpelier VT
properties.description: A 35-acre cemetery established in 1854, with 2.5 miles of winding terraced roads and notable sculptural gravestones — including a hand-carved granite staircase tomb and a life-size statue marking a child's grave. Final resting place for several Vermont governors and war heroes; includes a small 1865 Civil War soldiers' lot.
properties.detail:
Green Mount Cemetery

📍 250 State Street, Montpelier, VT

Established in 1854 on land partly funded by lawyer Calvin Keith, this 35-acre cemetery winds across 2.5 miles of terraced hillside roads. Notable for its sculptural craftsmanship — showcasing Vermont's granite and marble carving traditions, including the William Stowell tomb with hand-cut granite stairs and a life-size statue marking the 1900 grave of seven-year-old Margaret Pitkin. Several Vermont governors and war heroes are buried here, alongside a small 1865 Civil War soldiers' lot donated to the federal government.

Tips
- A quiet, atmospheric walk rather than a formal attraction — good for those interested in funerary art or Vermont history.
- Pairs naturally with the nearby Vermont State House.

properties.name: Green Mountain Railroad White River Junction VT
properties.description: Vermont's scenic excursion railroad, whose "White River Flyer" ran from White River Junction's Union Depot to Norwich and the Montshire Museum of Science along the Connecticut River. A historic 1892 steam engine, "Old 494," sits on display in Depot Park. Recent listings (Yelp, 2026) mark the White River Junction operation as closed — verify current status before planning a ride.
properties.detail:
Green Mountain Railroad (White River Junction)

📍 106 Railroad Row, White River Junction, VT

The Green Mountain Railroad runs three Vermont excursion routes; the White River Flyer departed Union Depot here for Norwich and the Montshire Museum of Science, tracing the Connecticut River with White Mountain foothill views and passing a causeway wildlife sanctuary. A historic 1892 steam engine, "Old 494," is displayed in the adjacent Depot Park.

Tips
- Recent listings mark the White River Junction operation as closed — verify current status before planning around it; the Green Mountain Railroad's other routes (Burlington–Charlotte, Bellows Falls–Chester) may still be running.
- Depot Park and "Old 494" are worth a quick look even if the excursion train isn't operating.

properties.detail:
GreenSpark Sustainability Park

📍 95 Gregg Hill Rd, Waterbury Center, VT

Opened in 2017 by owner Alex Chernomazov as the country's first interactive sustainability park — the whole site runs entirely off the electric grid on its own solar power. Exhibits let visitors explore renewable energy and green building hands-on, plus a "sustainable garage" showcasing vehicles powered by electricity, wind, and biomass.

Tips
- Closed on rainy days — check weather and call ahead.
- Guided tours run at 12pm, 2pm, and 4pm.

properties.name: Grindle Point Lighthouse Islesboro ME
properties.description: An 1850 lighthouse right at the Islesboro ferry landing (reached from Lincolnville), guarding the entrance to Gilkey Harbor. The keeper's quarters house the Sailors' Memorial Museum; the tower reopened to the public in June 2025 after a six-year closure for repairs.
properties.detail:
Grindle Point Lighthouse

📍 Islesboro Island, ME (ferry landing, ~6 miles from Lincolnville)

Appropriated in 1849 and rebuilt in 1875, this brick lighthouse guided ships into Gilkey Harbor during the 19th century, when Islesboro was home to many ship captains. Decommissioned in 1933, sold to the Town of Islesboro for $1,200 in 1934, and reactivated in 1987. The keeper's quarters now house the Sailors' Memorial Museum.

Tips
- Right next to the ferry landing — no car needed to visit.
- Tower reopened to the public June 29, 2025 after a six-year structural-repair closure.
- Museum open Friday–Sunday, July 1 through Labor Day — squarely within the trip window.

properties.name: Grindstone Neck Golf Course Winter Harbor ME
properties.description: A nine-hole course founded in 1891, one of the oldest in Maine, built as part of a Gilded Age summer community on Grindstone Neck. Every hole has a water view of Winter Harbor or Frenchman Bay's pink-granite shoreline. Redesigned by Alex Findlay in the early 1900s.
properties.detail:
Grindstone Neck Golf Course

📍 106 Grindstone Ave, Winter Harbor, ME

Founded in 1891 as part of a Gilded Age summer colony built by a group of Philadelphia and New York families — the Neck once had a 250-room inn, two churches, a casino, and a saltwater pool alongside the course. Alex Findlay redesigned the original holes in the early 1900s. The community faded after the Depression and WWII, then revived starting in the 1980s. Every hole on the nine-hole course has a water view of Winter Harbor or Frenchman Bay's pink granite coastline.

Tips
- A scenic round even for non-serious golfers, given the water views from every hole.
- Semi-private — check current public access/tee-time policy before planning around it.

Gritty's Brew Pub

Gritty's served their first beer — "Best Bitter" — in December of 1988 and continues to brew and serve delicious craft beer to this day.

The Portland Gritty's Brew Pub is located inside the "Oxnard Stores" block on Fore Street. You can still see the original brickwork and ceiling beams, which have held fast since the building was constructed in 1837.

properties.name: Groveton Covered Bridge Northumberland NH
properties.description: An 1852 Paddleford-truss covered bridge over the Upper Ammonoosuc River in Groveton — the last survivor of five covered bridges once in Northumberland, built from local spruce cut on Cape Horn Mountain. Carried traffic until 1939; now foot-traffic only.
properties.detail:
Groveton Covered Bridge

📍 Groveton village, Northumberland, NH

Built in 1852 by Captain Charles P. Richardson and his son from native spruce cut on nearby Cape Horn Mountain and milled locally, this 126-foot Paddleford-truss bridge (with arches) is the last of five covered bridges that once stood in Northumberland. It carried vehicle traffic over the Upper Ammonoosuc River until a new Route 3 bridge opened in 1939; restored in 1964–65 by Milton and Arnold Graton, and again in 2020. Open to foot traffic only today.

Tips
- A quick, easy walk-through stop in the middle of Groveton village.

properties.name: Guildhall Village Historic District VT
properties.description: Vermont's Northeast Kingdom's first-settled village and Essex County's shire town, centered on a square common formed by a bend in VT Route 102. Highlights include the 1851 Greek Revival county courthouse and 1844 Congregational church; remnants of an 1787 gristmill and a 1921 hydroelectric plant sit along the Connecticut River nearby. Listed on the National Register in 1980.
properties.detail:
Guildhall Village Historic District

📍 Guildhall, VT (across the Connecticut River from Northumberland, NH)

First settled in the 1780s when a dam and sawmill went up on the Connecticut River, Guildhall became the shire town of Essex County and the first village established in Vermont's Northeast Kingdom. The historic district centers on a square common formed by a bend in VT Route 102, ringed by the 1851 Greek Revival county courthouse, the 1844 Congregational church, and a former jail complex from around 1880. Along the riverbank nearby are the remains of the 1787 Ward Bailey Gristmill and a 1921 hydroelectric plant destroyed by fire in 1963. Listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1980.

Tips
- A quiet, essentially untouristed Vermont village green — a nice contrast stop if coming from the busier NH side of the river.

properties.name: Halfway Rock Lighthouse Casco Bay ME
properties.description: A 76-foot granite tower on a lone rock 11 miles east of Portland, marking the entrance to Casco Bay. Privately purchased in 2014 for $283,000 and restored by its owner.
properties.detail:
Halfway Rock Lighthouse

📍 Halfway Rock, ~11 miles east of Portland, ME (Casco Bay)

First lit August 15, 1871, after decades of petitions following shipwrecks in the area. The 76-foot conical granite tower was automated in 1975. It survived a devastating 1962 nor'easter and was privately purchased in 2014 for $283,000, undergoing extensive restoration since.

Tips
- Privately owned; grounds and tower closed to the public.
- View by boat or air — Rocky Coast Cruises out of Portland offers trips that pass it.

properties.name: Hamilton House South Berwick ME
properties.description: A grand 1785 Georgian mansion on a bluff over the Salmon Falls River, a National Historic Landmark for its maritime trade history and revival garden — operated by Historic New England.
properties.detail:
Hamilton House

📍 40 Vaughan's Lane, South Berwick, ME

A grand 1785 Georgian mansion set on a bluff over the Salmon Falls River, with 50 acres of grounds — a National Historic Landmark recognized for its maritime trade history and a notable revival garden. Owned and operated by Historic New England as a historic house museum.

Tips
- Open June 1–October 15, Friday–Sunday, 11am–4pm; the grounds themselves are open year-round.
- Admission is free for Historic New England members, $8 for non-members, with senior and group discounts.
- Combine with Hamilton House's near neighbor, the Sarah Orne Jewett House, also in South Berwick and also Historic New England-operated.
- A genuinely quiet, uncrowded stop compared to the more visited coastal Maine landmarks — worth it for the river-bluff setting alone.

properties.name: Hamlet of Staatsburg NY
properties.description: Stop 9 on the Hyde Park, Clinton & Pleasant Valley Scenic Tour. Thought to be the earliest settlement in Hyde Park, this hamlet along Old Post Rd. grew around commerce from farms and estates — Victorian-era houses, a former stage stop, and St. Margaret's Episcopal Church with French medieval stained glass.
properties.detail:
Hamlet of Staatsburg

📍 Old Post Rd, Staatsburg, NY 12580

Thought to be the earliest settlement in Hyde Park, this hamlet along Old Post Rd. was developed around commerce generated by farms and estates. The narrow lane, lined by trees and stone walls, passes the former Union Free School, wooden barns with unique trefoil and quadrifoil windows, Victorian-era houses, and a former stage stop. St. Margaret's Episcopal Church, a mid-19th-century English Gothic adaptation noted for its French medieval stained glass windows (a gift of Ogden Mills), sits nearby — its original home, a small Carpenter Gothic structure, now houses the Hamlet Library.

Tips
- Stop 9 of 26 on the Hyde Park, Clinton & Pleasant Valley Scenic Tour (Tour 3).

Harbor Dogs

A tiny red hot dog shack in Camden's municipal lot that takes hot dogs seriously and also nails fresh seafood — an unusual but well-executed combination. Rated 4.5 on Tripadvisor (#20 of 40 Camden restaurants), 4.4 on Google. Picnic tables right by the water, quick service, reasonable prices.

- Harbor Dog — the traditional Maine red hot dog with apple chutney

properties.name: Harbor Table Southwest Harbor ME
properties.detail:
Harbor Table is a casual dining restaurant located at 336 Main St, known for its friendly atmosphere and a variety of dishes including seafood and comfort foods. It attracts a diverse clientele, including locals and visitors, often groups looking for a comfortable dine-out experience. The vibe is casual, budget-friendly, and lively, making it suitable for casual gatherings and meals with friends or family.

Positives:  
- Excellent service and friendly staff  
- Delicious food with praises for specific dishes like sandwiches and dips  
- Cozy atmosphere that enhances the dining experience  
- Good variety of menu options

Common Issues:  
- Some reviews noted slow food service due to limited kitchen staff  
- A few customers felt that prices were a bit high for portion sizes  
- Occasionally, the quality of dishes can be inconsistent, with some items missing the mark  

Overall, Harbor Table is well-regarded for its service and food but faces challenges with food timing and price perceptions.

properties.name: Harborwalk Trail Portland ME
properties.description: A waterfront walk along Commercial Street past wharves, piers, working fishing boats, public art, and views into Casco Bay.
properties.detail:
Harborwalk Trail

Start at 53 Portland Pier — wander past J's Oyster to the pier's end for a view of DiMillo's floating restaurant and marina.

The Fore River winds along the Portland waterfront and into Casco Bay, bringing lobstermen, kayakers, and the occasional seal. Soak in the sights and sounds of Portland's working waterfront from the many wharves and piers along Commercial Street.

Highlights
- DiMillo's floating restaurant and marina at Portland Pier
- Waves & Anchor fence next to Portland Lobster Co. (great photo spot)
- Long Wharf with public art installations and historic monuments
- Views of Casco Bay and working lobster boats

Tips
- Best in the morning when the working waterfront is active
- The full harborwalk connects to Long Wharf and beyond

properties.detail:
Harpswell Meetinghouse

📍 Route 123, Harpswell Center, Harpswell, ME

Built starting in the late 1750s (not fully completed until the mid-1770s), this is the oldest surviving colonial meetinghouse in Maine — a simple, clapboard-sided, two-story building with a pulpit facing a three-sided gallery, typical of New England meetinghouse design. It served as both church and town hall from 1757 until the parish built a separate church across the road in 1843; the town took ownership in 1856 and it's still used for town meetings today. Designated a National Historic Landmark in 1968.

Tips
- The building itself is simple and unadorned — the significance is historical/architectural rather than a showpiece interior.
- For guided tour information, contact the Harpswell Historical Society directly (harpshistory@gmail.com) — it's not a staffed daily-visit site.
- Combine with the rest of Harpswell's historic sites; the Harpswell Historical Society maintains a broader list of the town's colonial-era locations.
- A quiet, low-key stop — good for a short detour rather than a dedicated half-day visit.

properties.name: Holy Resurrection Orthodox Church Berlin NH
properties.description: Built in 1915 by Russian immigrants — mostly from present-day Belarus and Ukraine — who came to work Berlin's lumber mills. Listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
properties.detail:
Holy Resurrection Orthodox Church

📍 20 Petrograd Street, Berlin, NH

Built in just five months in 1915, led by Reverend Arcady Piotrowsky, to serve the roughly 500 Russian immigrants then living in Berlin — mostly single men from the Minsk, Volyn, and Grodno provinces of what's now Belarus and Ukraine, drawn by the city's booming lumber industry. Mill strikes in the 1920s and the Great Depression in the 1930s drove many parishioners away in search of work elsewhere; the church closed in 1963 and sat dormant until reopening in 1974 for the funeral of a longtime Russian immigrant parishioner. Listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

Tips
- A distinctive onion-domed landmark that speaks to a little-known chapter of New Hampshire's immigrant labor history.

properties.detail:
Holy Resurrection Orthodox Church

📍 Claremont, NH

Founded in 1909 when the Brotherhood of the Holy Resurrection formed among Eastern European immigrants — mostly from the area between Moscow and Warsaw near the Polish border — who'd come to work Claremont's booming water-powered mills (paper, cloth, drills, mine and mill machinery). By 1914 the Brotherhood had 55 members and purchased a two-story house, converting the lower floor into a temporary church; an independent parish soon grew to 120 members. The current church building was completed in 1941. Listed on the New Hampshire State Register of Historic Places.

Tips
- Not to be confused with the identically-named Holy Resurrection Orthodox Church in Berlin, NH — a different parish, founded the same era by a different immigrant community (Russian mill workers rather than the mixed Eastern European community here), in a different part of the state.

properties.name: Hulls Cove Visitor Center Acadia National Park ME
properties.description: Acadia's main visitor center, just off Route 3 at the start of Park Loop Road — orientation film, park maps, ranger trip-planning advice, and the place to pick up entrance passes and Cadillac Summit Road reservations if not booked online.
properties.detail:
Hulls Cove Visitor Center

📍 Route 3, near the north entrance to Park Loop Road, Acadia National Park, ME

Acadia's primary visitor center, right at the start of Park Loop Road. Staffed by rangers who can help plan a route, check current trail/road conditions, and answer questions; shows a short park orientation film. The place to buy an entrance pass in person if you didn't get one online ahead of time.

Tips
- A natural first stop if starting the Park Loop Road drive from the Bar Harbor side.
- Gets busy midday in peak season — early morning is easiest for a quick in-and-out.

properties.name: Hunters Beach Acadia National Park ME
properties.description: A secluded cobblestone cove reached by a short forested walk, with a brook flowing through smooth, glacier- and wave-tumbled cobbles into the sea. The cobbles shift and clink musically as waves roll in and out — a quieter, less-visited alternative to Sand Beach.
properties.detail:
Hunters Beach

📍 Off Park Loop Road, near Seal Harbor, Acadia National Park, ME

A short, pleasant forested walk leads to a secluded cove covered in ocean-tumbled cobblestones, with a small brook running through the rocks into the sea. As the surf comes and goes, the cobbles shift and clink together — a distinctive, almost musical soundscape. Quieter and far less crowded than Sand Beach.

Tips
- Not a swimming beach — cold water and a rocky (not sandy) shore; come for the sound and scenery.
- Watch your footing on wet cobbles, which shift underfoot.

properties.name: Ice Caves Trail Cragsmoor NY
properties.description: The signature loop trail at Sam's Point Preserve, threading through the Ellenville Fault Ice Caves — deep fissures in the conglomerate rock where ice can linger into summer.
properties.detail:
Ice Caves Trail

📍 Sam's Point Preserve, Cragsmoor, NY

The main loop trail at Sam's Point Preserve, leading through the Ellenville Fault Ice Caves — a series of deep fissures and passageways in the conglomerate bedrock, cool enough that ice can linger well into summer. Often combined into a loop with Lake Maratanza, the highest lake on the ridge.

Tips
- Bring a flashlight and a layer — the caves stay cold even on hot days.
- Some passages involve ladders and tight squeezes; not ideal for claustrophobia.
- Pairs naturally with a Lake Maratanza loop from the same Sam's Point trailhead.

properties.detail:
Indian Island Lighthouse

📍 Rockport Harbor, Rockport, ME

Congress appropriated funds in 1849 for a lighthouse at the entrance to Rockport Harbor. Discontinued in 1859 due to proximity to other lights, then restored in 1875 as lime shipping revived the harbor's traffic. Operated until 1933, then sold at auction in 1934 for $1,025 to a Chicago buyer — it's remained in the same family since, and appeared in the 2001 film In the Bedroom.

Tips
- Privately owned, no public access.
- Best viewed from the water via Camden Harbor Cruises, or from shore near Rockport.

Isle au Haut Ferry Stonington ME
properties.description: The Isle au Haut Boat Services mail boat departs Stonington daily for the 45-minute crossing to Isle au Haut — a remote island where roughly a third of the land is a wild and almost entirely undeveloped section of Acadia National Park. The NPS limits day visitors to 48 people per day; advance reservations required May through October.
properties.detail:
Isle au Haut Ferry

📍 Stonington ME

The Isle au Haut Boat Services mail boat departs Stonington daily for the 45-minute crossing to Isle au Haut — a remote island where roughly a third of the land is a wild and almost entirely undeveloped section of Acadia National Park. The NPS limits day visitors to 48 people per day; advance reservations required May through October.

Tips
- Reserve NPS day-use permits well in advance at recreation. — they sell out weeks ahead.
- The ferry drops at Town Landing; the NPS section is a 4-mile walk or bike ride south at Duck Harbor.
- Bring everything you need — the island has almost no services for day visitors.
- The remoteness and quiet are the point: this is what the rest of Acadia looked like before the crowds.

properties.name: Isle au Haut Lighthouse Isle au Haut ME
properties.description: A 1907 granite-and-brick lighthouse on Robinson Point, guiding fishing vessels into Isle au Haut's harbor. Owned by the Town of Isle au Haut since 1998; reach it by ferry from Stonington.
properties.detail:
Isle au Haut Lighthouse (Robinson Point)

📍 Robinson Point, Isle au Haut, ME

Completed December 30, 1907, this 40-foot granite and brick tower with a fifth-order Fresnel lens guided fishing boats into the harbor during fierce northeast snowstorms. Only two head keepers ever served here before automation in 1933. The Town of Isle au Haut took ownership in 1998 and led a major restoration in 2021.

Tips
- Reach via the Isle au Haut ferry from Stonington, then walk to the point; grounds open, dwelling and tower closed.
- Isle au Haut Boat Services runs scheduled trips that include a view of the lighthouse.

- Local seafood prepared fresh
- The pier setting offers stunning mountain and water views

properties.name: JB Brown Memorial Block Portland ME
properties.description: One of the few commercial buildings in Portland designed in the Queen Anne style, favoring fine details, asymmetry, and broken rooflines more commonly associated with residential architecture.
properties.detail:
J.B. Brown Memorial Block

📍 Congress Street & Casco Street, Portland, ME

The J.B. Brown Memorial Block at Congress and Casco Streets is one of the few commercial buildings in Portland designed in the Queen Anne style. This style — which favors fine details, asymmetry, and broken rooflines — was more commonly applied to residential buildings, making this block a rare commercial example.

Fun fact: Many of Portland's historic buildings display two dates — the older is when originally constructed, and the newer is when reconstructed after the Great Fire of 1866.

properties.detail:
Jackson Corners & Gaddes Store

Jackson Corners was an important stop on the Nobletown stage road to northern New England before the end of the 18th century. Gaddes Store (1773) was one of many inns along the route, spaced roughly ten miles apart so horses could be changed and passengers allowed to stretch. A few hundred feet into Columbia County leads to the Taconic Parkway.

Tips

properties.description: Quiet contemplative garden space on Camden Public Library grounds, adjoining the Children's Garden—rarely mentioned in guidebooks but designed as a peaceful memorial space.

Jean S. Picker Memorial Garden & Children's Garden

A smaller, quieter garden space on the Camden Public Library grounds, adjoining a Children's Garden — part of the same library complex as the better-known Amphitheatre & Fawn's Garden (the Fletcher Steele-designed horseshoe theater), but a distinct, smaller corner of it. Worth noting: independent research on this specific garden by name is thin online — most sources reference the library's "Jean Picker Room" (an indoor space) rather than a standalone outdoor garden, so treat the exact scope here as approximate until seen in person.

Tips

- If it turns out to be the same space as the Amphitheatre/Fawn's Garden rather than a distinct corner, that's fine — either way it's worth the short walk from Main Street.

properties.name: Jeffersonville Bridge Cambridge VT
properties.description: Also known as the Cambridge Junction (Poland) Bridge — a 152.5-foot Burr arch truss covered bridge over the Lamoille River, built 1887 by George W. Holmes to give communities west of the river access to the railroad station. Listed on the National Register in 1974; restored 2001 (stabilized and raised 3 feet).
properties.detail:
Jeffersonville Bridge

📍 Cambridge Junction Road, off Route 15, Cambridge, VT

Also known as the Cambridge Junction Bridge or Poland Covered Bridge, this 152.5-foot, one-lane Burr arch truss span over the Lamoille River was built in 1887 by George Washington Holmes, giving communities west of the river access to the Cambridge Junction railroad station. Combines an arch-bridge design with King Post-style trusswork. Listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1974; underwent a two-stage restoration in 2001 that stabilized and raised the structure three feet.

Tips
- A classic Vermont covered-bridge photo stop, off the main Route 15 corridor.

properties.name: Jericho Mountain State Park Berlin NH
properties.description: New Hampshire's only major state-owned ATV riding area — 50-60 miles of OHV trails, plus the first public-land 4x4 Jeep/truck trail in the Northeast (an official Jeep Badge of Honor route). Connects to 1,000+ miles of Coös County OHRV trails reaching Gorham, Errol, Pittsburg, and beyond without trailering. Campground and a swimming beach on site.
properties.detail:
Jericho Mountain State Park

📍 Berlin, NH

Acquired by the state in 2005 and redesigned around motorized recreation, this is New Hampshire's only major state-owned ATV riding area — 50 to 60 miles of trail for ATVs, UTVs, trail bikes, and snowmobiles, plus the first public-land 4x4 Jeep and truck trail in the Northeast, an official Jeep off-roading Badge of Honor route. Riders can connect straight into 1,000+ miles of Coös County OHRV trails, reaching Gorham, Errol, Pittsburg, and even Maine and Vermont without trailering. The campground has 20 sites (including cabins and Adirondack shelters) with a modern shower/laundry building, plus a day-use beach and boat launch.

Tips
- Bring your own OHV — this is a trail network, not a rental operation on site (check locally for nearby rental options if needed).
- The 4x4 trail is a genuine technical off-road route, not a casual scenic drive — know your vehicle's capability first.

properties.name: John Innes Kane Cottage Bar Harbor ME

properties.detail:
John Innes Kane Cottage

📍 Bar Harbor, ME

A Gilded Age "cottage" built for the Kane family, one of Bar Harbor's prominent turn-of-the-century summer residents, listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

Tips
- Private property — a drive/walk-past landmark, not a stop with public access.

Story (Shore Path stop 8)

Now you're at the southern stretch of the walk, and this is one of the best-preserved cottages you'll pass — Tudor-style, built in nineteen-oh-three and nineteen-oh-four for John Innes Kane, whose own great-grandfather was John Jacob Astor, once the richest man in America. Kane didn't work; the New York Times once described his interests as "scientific matters, especially those dealing with discovery and exploration." He married Annie Cottenet Schermerhorn in a wedding gown made by the famous Parisian designer Charles Frederick Worth, and died in New York in nineteen thirteen.

Unlike most of the architects on this walk, who came from Boston and New York, Kane's house was designed by a local man — Fred L. Savage, Bar Harbor's own architect, working for some of the wealthiest families in the country. And unlike Shore Acres, the original Grant cottage, or so many of the others you've passed, this one is a genuine survivor: it's one of only a small number of Bar Harbor estate houses that made it through the devastating fire of nineteen forty-seven still standing. It's private property and it's listed on the National Register of Historic Places, so admire it from the path rather than the driveway.

properties.description: Casual breakfast and lunch diner in Bar Harbor known for wild Maine blueberry pancakes and lobster rolls.
properties.detail:
Open in Google Maps

What It Is & What It's Best Known For

Jordan's Restaurant is a casual breakfast and lunch diner on Cottage Street in Bar Harbor, Maine. It is unpretentious and long known for its wild Maine blueberry pancakes. The menu includes lobster rolls, omelets (Maine delight, lobster cheese, western), quiche, waffles, home fries, bacon, and clam chowder. The restaurant celebrates its 50th anniversary in 2026.

Typical Customers

The restaurant attracts tourists (especially those visiting Cadillac Mountain for sunrise), families with children, locals who view it as "the heart of this town," and travelers seeking affordable, no-frills breakfast experiences.

Overall Vibe

Casual and bustling with a "small-town feel" and "old school vibe." The atmosphere is informal and fast-paced—customers are told to "sit wherever you like." The energy is lively with staff "hustling and enjoying their work." Decidedly budget-friendly and unpretentious, described as "no frills, no foam art, just real food."

Strongest Positives (from reviews)

1. Wild Maine blueberry pancakes are exceptional – Mentioned in 393 reviews, guests consistently praise them as "delicious" and "exceptional." The wild Maine blueberries are "tiny but so flavorful." Blueberry muffins and waffles are similarly praised as "loaded with blueberries."
    
2. Outstanding value and affordability – Reviewers call it "the best and probably cheapest breakfast" in town. At $10–20 per person, the generous portions deliver excellent value. One reviewer noted it as "the best and probably cheapest breakfast we had while in town."
    
3. Genuinely friendly staff and welcoming local character – Staff are described as "very kind," "super friendly," and helpful with local tips. The owner and crew are viewed as a "family" that treats both locals and visitors with warmth. One local called it "definitely this gem" and "the heart of this town."
    
4. Excellent omelets and diverse menu beyond blueberries – Omelets (Maine delight, lobster cheese, lobster mushroom) are consistently praised as "delicious." Quiche, lobster rolls, home fries, bacon, and clam chowder receive positive mentions for quality and portion size.
    

Most Common Issues or Downsides (from reviews)

1. High-volume service creates pressure and inconsistency – One reviewer with a young child reported "bad" service and felt "pressured to be quick and get out as soon as possible." Another noted the place is "so busy that we felt pressured to be quick." The owner acknowledged poor service "is not the norm," but the volume operation can affect the dining pace.
    
2. Some menu items fall short – Haddock chowder was described as "way too watery and quite disappointing." One reviewer found blueberry pancakes "way overhyped" and "ok" rather than exceptional, noting they "are not sweet."
    
3. Popularity creates crowds and waits – The restaurant is extremely busy during peak times, which contributes to the rushed atmosphere despite the casual seating policy.

properties.detail:

Built in 1793 for Joseph Marsh, one of Hartford's early settlers, who led a regiment of colonial militia in the Revolutionary War, helped draft the 1777 constitution of the independent Vermont Republic, and served as Vermont's first Lieutenant Governor under Thomas Chittenden. His son Charles, a noted lawyer, was raised here and later fathered conservationist George Perkins Marsh. The complex — main house, three barns, and a wagon shed/hen house — was moved a short distance in the 1960s due to an Army Corps of Engineers flood-control project. Now operates as the Quechee Inn. Tips

properties.detail:
Libby Island Lighthouse

📍 Libby Island, Machiasport, ME (entrance to Machias Bay)

The original stone tower, built in the summer and fall of 1822, collapsed within months from poor workmanship and frozen mortar; Noah Humphrey rebuilt it soon after. Libby Island earned its reputation as America's foggiest lighthouse station, averaging 1,554 fog hours annually, which required a large keeper staff and heavy fog-signal infrastructure. Automated and transferred to the Maine Coastal Islands National Wildlife Refuge in 1998.

Tips
- Grounds and tower closed to the public — best seen by boat through Bold Coast Charters or Bar Harbor Whale Watch.
- Far Down East; a full-day undertaking from Bar Harbor.

The summit offers 360-degree views of the Kinsman Range, Cannon Cliffs, Franconia Notch, and the Pemigewasset Wilderness. The Liberty Spring Tentsite, about 1.5 miles up, is a popular overnight stop with platforms and reliable water.

Tips

- CRITICAL: Time this around low tide only. Check tide charts before planning.

properties.detail:
Little River Lighthouse

📍 Little River Island, Cutler, ME

Congress appropriated funds in 1847 for a conical stone tower to reduce shipwrecks in this fog-prone stretch of coast; an iron tower replaced it in 1876. Automated in 1975 and left to deteriorate until the American Lighthouse Foundation restored the lantern room in 2001, then took ownership in 2002 — the first lighthouse transfer of its kind in New England.

Tips
- Grounds open June–October when the floating dock is in place; overnight stays available in the restored keeper's house through Friends of Little River Lighthouse.
- Occasional summer open houses include transportation to the island and tower access.

CCC Camp Smith once housed 2,000 men here in 80+ buildings — only scattered chimneys and foundations remain today, some marked on a self-guided history trail.
properties.detail:
Little River State Park Campground

📍 Waterbury Reservoir, Waterbury, VT

Built in the wake of Vermont's catastrophic November 1927 flood, which killed 55 people and caused over $22 million in damage statewide. Between 1935 and 1938, the Civilian Conservation Corps built Waterbury Dam and Reservoir alongside the Army Corps of Engineers to control future flooding — and housed the workforce in CCC Camp Smith, a fully self-contained community of over 80 buildings holding up to 2,000 men, complete with a hospital, theater, school, church, and ice rink. Only scattered chimneys and concrete foundations remain today, some marked along a self-guided history trail through the park.

Tips
- One of central Vermont's most popular parks — reserve well ahead for camping in peak season.
- Combine with a paddle or swim on Waterbury Reservoir itself.

First exhibited December 31, 1890, to mark the newly dredged channel — one of only three remaining "spark plug"/"wedding cake" style caisson lights on the Maine coast. properties.name: Lutheran Stone Church Red Hook NY
properties.description: Stop 28 on the Rhinebeck, Red Hook & Milan Scenic Tour. This 1786 structure replaces a log church ca. 1730 and housed a congregation dating back to the Palatine immigration of 1715.
properties.detail:
Lutheran Stone Church

📍 Route 9, Red Hook, NY

This 1786 structure replaces a log church ca. 1730 and housed a congregation dating back to the Palatine immigration of 1715.

Tips
- Stop 28 of 33 on the Rhinebeck, Red Hook & Milan Scenic Tour (Tour 1).

Quick Read
- Built: 1786 — stone replacement for a ca. 1730 log structure.
- Congregation: Continuous since the Palatine immigration of 1715 — one of the oldest Lutheran flocks in the Hudson Valley.
- Style: Vernacular stone, austere, fortress-squat — exactly what you'd expect from cash-strapped German immigrants who'd outlasted persecution and wilderness.
- Stop 28/33 on the Rhinebeck, Red Hook & Milan Scenic Tour (Tour 1).

Vibe
Plain, pious, and proud. No spires begging the sky — just thick walls holding three centuries of Palatine memory. Worth a pull-off; photographers will like the texture, historians will like the timeline.

One-Liner
"1786 stone; 1730 log beneath it; 1715 souls beneath that — Route 9's quiet Palatine witness."

properties.name: Machias Seal Island Lighthouse Cutler ME
properties.description: An 1832 lighthouse on a remote island claimed by both the US and Canada, ~12 miles off Cutler. Home to the largest Atlantic puffin colony south of the Gulf of St. Lawrence; visited via puffin-watching boat tours.
properties.detail:
Machias Seal Island Lighthouse

📍 Machias Seal Island, ~12 miles off Cutler, ME (also claimed by Canada)

Both the U.S. and Canada have claimed sovereignty over this island. The original wooden octagonal towers date to 1832; a third-order Fresnel lens was added in 1869 and a powerful steam fog whistle — the strongest then on the Bay of Fundy — in 1873. The current reinforced concrete tower, built in 1915, is still active. The island hosts the largest Atlantic puffin nesting colony south of the Gulf of St. Lawrence.

Tips
- Visited via puffin tours from Bold Coast Charters (Cutler) or Sea Watch Tours (Grand Manan, Canada); landing is weather-dependent.
- Bar Harbor Whale Watch also runs lighthouse excursions past the island.
- Book puffin tours well ahead — they sell out during nesting season, which overlaps the trip window.

properties.name: Mackworth Island Falmouth ME
properties.description: A 1.5-mile loop trail circling a small island in Casco Bay, connected to Falmouth by a short causeway — stunning 360° views of the bay, Portland skyline, and islands with almost no elevation gain. One of Maine's most rewarding short walks.
properties.detail:
Mackworth Island

📍 Andrews Avenue causeway, Falmouth, ME (~10 min from downtown Portland)

Mackworth Island is a small state-owned island in Casco Bay connected to Falmouth by a short causeway. The perimeter trail — a 1.5-mile loop — hugs the rocky shoreline almost the entire way, offering 360° views of the bay, the Portland skyline, the Calendar Islands, and the open Atlantic.

The walk is virtually flat, takes about 40 minutes at a leisurely pace, and is consistently rated among the best short walks in Maine. The island also features a fairy house village in the woods near the center — a whimsical tradition maintained by local children.

Tips
- A Maine state park vehicle pass ($8 non-resident day use) is required at the gate; cash or card accepted
- Arrive before 9 AM on summer weekends — the small parking area fills up fast
- The causeway itself offers good views of Portland Harbor before you even reach the island
- Combine with a Portland Head Light visit (~15 min south) for a full morning outdoors
- Dogs welcome on leash

properties.name: Mad River Glen Waitsfield VT
properties.description: A skier-owned cooperative — the only one in the US — known for natural snow, low skier density, and a deliberately non-commercial atmosphere ("Ski it if you can"). Home to one of only two operating single-person chairlifts left in the country, running since 1948 and fully restored in 2007 with $1.8 million raised by 1,700+ shareholders.
properties.detail:
Mad River Glen

📍 62 Mad River Glen Resort Road, Fayston, VT (near Waitsfield)

Skier-owned since 1995 — the first, and still the only, cooperatively-owned ski area in the United States. That ownership structure shapes the whole experience: low skier density, natural snow prioritized over snowmaking, and a deliberately non-commercial, old-school feel ("Ski it if you can" is the unofficial motto). Its Single Chair, in continuous operation since 1948, is one of only two single-person chairlifts still running in the country (the other is in Cordova, Alaska). Over 80% of the 1,700+ shareholders voted to restore it rather than replace it, raising $1.8 million; the refurbished lift reopened December 15, 2007.

Tips
- Known for genuinely challenging, natural terrain — not the resort to pick if you want groomed cruisers and snowmaking guarantees.
- Right by Appalachian Gap, so easy to combine both stops on a Route 17 drive.

Also functions as an event space (drag shows, concerts, poetry readings). Post-pandemic, open by appointment or during events only.
properties.detail:
Main Street Museum

📍 White River Junction, VT (former fire station, Bridge Street)

Founded in 1992 by career artist David Fairbanks Ford in "The Old South End," inspired by 18th-century cabinets of curiosities. The collection is deliberately unfocused: taxidermy and biological anomalies (dehydrated cats among them), miniature shoes, a huge collected-key display, sheet music, journals, electromagnetic devices, Elvis impersonator memorabilia — and genuinely odd specifics like Elvis Presley's gallstones, presidential hair clippings, and dirt from outside Charles Lindbergh's house. Housed in the town's former fire station, next to the railroad underpass on the White River.

Tips
- Open by appointment or during events only since the pandemic — check ahead rather than dropping by unannounced.
- A genuinely odd, memorable stop if you can time it right — not a conventional museum experience.

A 20-acre waterfront campus centered on the Percy & Small Shipyard, designated a National Historic Landmark in 1994 as the only surviving U.S. shipyard that built large wooden sailing vessels — 42 giant wooden schooners were launched here between 1894 and 1920, including the Wyoming (1909), the largest wooden sailing ship ever built in America. The broader museum covers Maine's shipbuilding and maritime history well beyond just the shipyard itself.

Must See

properties.name: Matinicus Rock Lighthouse Knox County ME
properties.description: A remote 1827 lighthouse (rebuilt 1857) 27 miles from Rockland, famous as the site of teenage keeper's daughter Abbie Burgess's heroic month alone tending the lights during an 1856 gale.
properties.detail:
Matinicus Rock Lighthouse

📍 Matinicus Rock, ~27 miles from Rockland, ME

Built in 1827 with twin wooden towers, rebuilt in granite in 1846, and again in 1857. Famous for 17-year-old Abbie Burgess, who single-handedly kept the lights burning for a month during a devastating 1856 gale while her father was ashore: "Under God I was able to perform all my accustomed duties as well as my father's." Waves have been known to wash over structures 48 feet above high water — one of the most exposed light stations on the Atlantic Coast.

Tips
- Closed to the public; owned by U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service as part of the Maine Coastal Islands National Wildlife Refuge.
- Boat or air access only — Matinicus Excursions runs occasional trips.
- A Fresnel lens from the station is on display at the Maine Lighthouse Museum in Rockland.

McLoon's Lobster Shack

properties.name: McLoons Lobster Shack South Thomaston ME
properties.description: A tiny red-shingled hut on Spruce Head Island right beside a working lobster wharf — widely called the best lobster roll in the area, watched over by the boats that just caught it.
properties.detail:
McLoons Lobster Shack

📍 315 Island Rd, Spruce Head, South Thomaston, ME

A small, red-shingled lobster shack right on a working wharf on Spruce Head Island, a few miles south of Rockland — picnic tables sit close enough to watch lobster boats unloading their catch while you eat. Rated 4.7 on Tripadvisor (#1 of 5 restaurants in South Thomaston), 4.6 on Restaurant Guru across nearly 4,000 reviews, and 4.8 on Sirved — consistently among the most-praised lobster rolls in the Midcoast.

Must Order
- Lobster roll — generously filled, repeatedly called the best reviewers have ever had
- Blueberry bread pudding — a genuine standout dessert, best served warmed

Tips
- Expect a line at peak lunch hours — it's a small operation and popular.
- Lobster rolls run $15+; this isn't the cheapest option, but reviewers consistently say it's worth it.
- The working-wharf setting is part of the appeal — arrive ready to watch the boats, not just eat.

properties.name: McSeagull's Restaurant Boothbay Harbor ME
properties.description: Lively harborfront spot famous for its lobster roll and award-winning clam chowder.
properties.detail:
McSeagull's Restaurant

📍 14 Wharf St, Boothbay Harbor, ME

A pub-style harborfront institution built right over the water next to Boothbay Harbor's famous footbridge, with both indoor dining and a wraparound outdoor deck that's one of the best harbor-view seats in town. Ranked among the top 20 of 50+ Boothbay Harbor restaurants across hundreds of reviews, with a Tripadvisor Certificate of Excellence. The menu leans pub-casual — lobster dishes, fresh seafood, burgers, pizza, nachos — rather than fine dining, which is exactly the appeal after a day on the water.

Must Order
- Lobster roll — a generous portion of whole lobster meat, the dish most reviewers single out
- Award-winning clam chowder — repeatedly called out as some of the best in New England; pair with the lobster bisque if you can't choose

Tips
- Busy in peak season — expect a wait at lunch and prime dinner hours; outdoor deck seating goes first.
- Price range runs roughly $12–$40, wide enough to work for a casual lunch or a full seafood dinner.
- Ask for a table on the deck side facing the footbridge — the view is the draw as much as the food.

Two rock-dam crossings over Meadow Brook require careful stone-stepping.
properties.detail:
Meadow Brook Preserve

- Watch footing at the two rock-dam brook crossings mid-trail

properties.name: Mechanics Hall Portland ME
properties.description: A communal gathering hall built 1857–1859 by the Maine Charitable Mechanic Association, featuring a grand ballroom, member library, and historic classroom; today a cultural hub for literary arts, music, and performance.
properties.detail:
Mechanics' Hall

📍 519 Congress Street, Portland, ME

In 1815, the Maine Charitable Mechanic Association was formed to support Maine's creative community — blacksmiths, coopers, artists, innovators, and creators. Between 1857 and 1859, they built Mechanics' Hall at 519 Congress Street as a communal gathering space with a lending library at its center.

Today, Mechanics' Hall celebrates that rich history through literary arts programs, music, performance, and more while working to restore the landmark building as a vibrant cultural resource.

Inside you'll find:
- A grand ballroom
- A member-supported library
- A historic classroom

properties.name: Megunticook Falls Camden ME

Megunticook Market and Catering

📍 2 Gould St, Camden, ME

A neighborhood market and deli that also runs a serious catering operation — good selection of meats, local produce, an eclectic sandwich menu, plus pizza and pre-made meals for a quick grab. Rated 4.4 on Restaurant Guru, #23 of 41 Camden restaurants on Tripadvisor. Reviews are genuinely mixed: strong on the deli/catering side, more inconsistent on the pre-made and online-order side.

- Locally sourced produce and meats if you're provisioning rather than eating on-site

properties.name: Mesier Park Wappingers Falls, NY
properties.description: A five-and-a-half-acre village green in Wappingers Falls built around the 18th-century Mesier Homestead.
properties.detail:
Mesier Park

📍 2 Spring St, Wappingers Falls, NY 12590

A shaded village green on a hill above Wappinger Creek, centered on the Mesier Homestead — a wood-frame house built in two phases, starting around 1741-42 and expanded in the 1750s. Peter Mesier bought the property in 1777, and the family sold it to the village in 1891 for public use. The park is a contributing feature of the Wappingers Falls Historic District, listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1984.

Tips
- The Homestead itself is run by the Wappingers Historical Society and opens for public tours one Sunday a month (typically 1, 2, and 3pm) — check their calendar before planning around it.
- A quick, easy stop to pair with Fishkill Historic District or Van Wyck Homestead on the way through — all a short drive apart along Route 9.

properties.name: Mill Village Historic District Waterbury VT
properties.description: A small 19th-century industrial village on Stowe Street, once powered by Graves (Thatcher's) Brook — mills and small industry thrived here into the 20th century. Most surviving buildings date 1860-1890; now a quiet residential area. Listed on the National Register in 1979.
properties.detail:
Mill Village Historic District

📍 Stowe Street, Waterbury, VT

A compact 19th-century industrial village along Stowe Street, once powered by the waters of Graves (also called Thatcher's) Brook, where a cluster of mills and small industrial operations thrived well into the 20th century. Most of the surviving residential buildings date from 1860 to 1890. Now a quiet residential pocket of Waterbury. Listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1979.

Tips
- A quiet residential walk, not a commercial attraction — appreciate it as a stroll through 19th-century mill-town architecture.

properties.name: Millbrook Village NY
properties.description: Stop 5 on the Washington & Amenia Scenic Tour. Flourished as a 19th-century railroad center; tree-lined Franklin Ave. invites strollers to galleries, antique shops, bookstores, restaurants and the Tribute Gardens.
properties.detail:
Millbrook Village

📍 Franklin Ave, Millbrook, NY 12545

Flourished as a result of local businessmen such as George H. Brown, owner of the United States Condensing Co. (est. 1864), who brought in the Newburgh, Dutchess & Columbia RR in 1869. Tree-lined Franklin Ave. invites strollers to galleries, antique shops, bookstores, restaurants and attractions such as the Tribute Gardens, a gift of Mrs. Oakleigh Thorne dedicated to WWI and WWII veterans. The Thorne Building, now a branch of Dutchess Community College, was intended as a school and cultural center.

Tips
- Park in lots or along streets and walk Franklin Ave.
- Stop 5 of 17 on the Washington & Amenia Scenic Tour (Tour 4) — this is the tour's namesake village, the hub of local government, business and culture.

properties.name: Millbrook Vineyards and Winery NY
properties.description: Stop 8 on the Washington & Amenia Scenic Tour. A critically acclaimed 130-acre estate winery, open year-round, with complimentary guided tours of the winemaking process.
properties.detail:
Millbrook Vineyards and Winery

📍 26 Wing Road, Millbrook, NY 12545

A critically acclaimed 130-acre estate winery, founded 1982 by John Dyson, open year-round with complimentary and informative tours offering an insider's view of the entire winemaking process. Cabernet Franc, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Tocai Friulano, and Riesling among the estate wines.

Tips
- Call 845/677-8383 or 800/662-WINE for visitor information — www.millbrookwine.com.
- Take a break from driving with a guided tour and wine tasting; world-class wines paired with amazing views.
- Stop 8 of 17 on the Washington & Amenia Scenic Tour (Tour 4).
- Marked purple on curatorial judgment, not a numeric Rating — 94% Facebook recommend (2,740 reviews), voted Best Winery in the Hudson Valley 30 consecutive years. No confirmed Google or TripAdvisor star figure found.

Mimi's on the Beach

A family-owned restaurant right inside Pemaquid Beach Park, tracing back to a 1980s beach shack run by the founders' mother. Serves seafood, burgers, sandwiches, and a kids menu — casual, right off the sand.

- Natural pairing with a beach day at Pemaquid Beach Park.

An unincorporated village on the shore of Mirror Lake in southern Tuftonboro, along NH Route 109 connecting Wolfeboro to Melvin Village and Moultonborough. properties.name: Mixed Greens Camden ME

Mixed Greens

properties.name: Moffat House Berlin NH
properties.description: The former home and office of Dr. and Mrs. Irving Moffett, now the Berlin and Coös County Historical Society's free museum — sports memorabilia, military uniforms (WWI through Desert Storm), a genealogy and records archive, and Dr. Moffett's preserved period medical office downstairs.
properties.detail:
Moffett House Museum

📍 119 High St, Berlin, NH

The former home and medical office of Dr. and Mrs. Irving Moffett, now run by the Berlin and Coös County Historical Society (opened as a museum in 1997). The main floor displays sports memorabilia and photo albums; upstairs holds three rooms of genealogy records and local town histories; downstairs, Dr. Moffett's original office and exam rooms are preserved with period medical equipment. The collection also includes military uniforms spanning WWI through Desert Storm and Coös County's largest collection of souvenir china.

Tips
- Free admission; open Tuesday–Saturday, 12–4pm.
- A good stop for anyone with North Country family genealogy to research.

properties.detail:
Mohonk Mountain House

📍 New Paltz, NY

A turreted seven-story resort stretching nearly an eighth of a mile along Lake Mohonk. The Sky Top tower, completed in 1923, offers views of six states on clear days. Distinct from (but adjacent to and historically connected with) the nonprofit Mohonk Preserve.

Tips
- Located off Mountain Rest Road, linking High Falls to the north and New Paltz to the south
- 35 miles of cross-country ski trails; 18,000 sq ft ice rink built in 2001
- Carriage roads built at the turn of the century are wonderfully preserved for hiking and biking

properties.name: Moose Peak Lighthouse Mistake Island ME
properties.description: An 1826 granite lighthouse on Mistake Island near Jonesport, once recorded as the foggiest spot in the US (1,562 fog hours in 1931). Privately owned but grounds open via a Nature Conservancy boardwalk.
properties.detail:
Moose Peak Lighthouse (Mistake Island)

📍 Mistake Island, ~5 miles southeast of Jonesport, ME

Built by Jeremy Berry and lit October 9, 1826, marking the entrance to Main Channel Way. First keeper Alexander Milliken, a War of 1812 privateer, served 23 years. In 1931 the station logged 1,562 fog hours — recognized as the foggiest spot in the country that year. Automated in 1972; sold into private hands in 2012 and again in 2019.

Tips
- Grounds open; landing on Nature Conservancy-controlled Mistake Island is allowed if visitors stay on the boardwalk to the lighthouse. Tower closed.
- Reach via local boat operators out of Jonesport.

properties.name: Moss Glen Falls Granville VT

A short (0.1-mile), easy walk from the parking area leads to a wooden viewing deck. Distinct from the other "Moss Glen Falls" in Stowe, VT.
properties.detail:
Moss Glen Falls (Granville)

📍 Route 100, Granville Gulf, Granville, VT

Formed where Deer Hollow Brook squeezes through a narrow bedrock notch and fans out into a remarkably symmetrical 68-foot veil — arguably the most photographed waterfall in Vermont, and easily one of the most accessible. Right along Route 100 within the Granville Gulf State Reservation; a large roadside parking area leads across a small bridge to a short (0.1-mile), easy walkway ending at a wooden viewing deck.

Tips
- Not the same waterfall as "Moss Glen Falls" in Stowe, VT — this vault has a separate note for that one; don't confuse the two when planning.
- Extremely popular — expect company, especially during foliage season.
